title: FFAvatar: Few-Shot, Feed-Forward, and Generalizable Avatar Reconstruction
summary: Avatar reconstruction has traditionally relied on per-subject optimization that requires hours of computation or on expensive preprocessing that limits scalability. We introduce FFAvatar, a generalizable feed-forward framework that reconstructs high-quality, animatable 3D Gaussian head avatars from few-shot unposed portrait images in seconds. FFAvatar fuses information from multiple source images into a unified canonical Gaussian representation through Multi-View Query-Former, which is animated via FLAME parameters predicted end-to-end directly from pixels, eliminating the overhead of offline FLAME extraction. We further propose a three-stage training curriculum that achieves both broad generalization and high-fidelity reconstruction: (i) scalable pretraining on extensive monocular video data with over 1M identities to learn strong generalizable priors; (ii) multi-view fine-tuning on a small but high-quality dataset of 360-degree captures to enhance geometric fidelity and extreme-view awareness; and (iii) optional personalization that adapts to specific identities for maximum fidelity within 500 optimization steps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FFAvatar sets a new standard for identity preservation, geometric consistency, and animation fidelity. On the NeRSemble benchmark, it outperforms the state-of-the-art LAM by a substantial 5.5 PSNR gain. Furthermore, FFAvatar enables real-time deployment, reconstructing avatars in 2 seconds without personalization and 10 seconds with personalization, while supporting 49 FPS animation on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

AI.tldr: FFAvatar is a feed-forward framework that reconstructs high-quality, animatable 3D Gaussian head avatars from few-shot unposed portrait images in seconds, eliminating per-subject optimization and expensive preprocessing through a three-stage training curriculum.
AI.motivation: Traditional avatar reconstruction relies on hours of per-subject optimization or expensive preprocessing, which limits scalability. There is a need for a fast, generalizable approach that can reconstruct high-quality animatable avatars from minimal input.
AI.method: FFAvatar uses Multi-View Query-Former to fuse multiple source images into a unified canonical Gaussian representation. It animates avatars via FLAME parameters predicted end-to-end from pixels (eliminating offline extraction). The three-stage training includes: (1) scalable pretraining on 1M+ identities from monocular video, (2) multi-view fine-tuning on 360-degree captures for geometric fidelity, and (3) optional personalization in 500 steps for maximum fidelity.
AI.result: FFAvatar sets new standards in identity preservation, geometric consistency, and animation fidelity. On the NeRSemble benchmark, it outperforms SOTA LAM by 5.5 PSNR. It achieves real-time deployment: 2 seconds reconstruction without personalization, 10 seconds with personalization, and supports 49 FPS animation on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.
AI.conclusion: FFAvatar enables efficient, high-quality avatar reconstruction that can be deployed in real-time, overcoming the scalability limitations of traditional methods while maintaining superior visual quality and animation fidelity.

title: FLASH: Efficient Visuomotor Policy via Sparse Sampling
summary: Generative models such as diffusion and flow matching have become dominant paradigms for visuomotor policy learning, yet their reliance on iterative denoising incurs high inference latency incompatible with real-time robotic control. We present Fast Legendre-polynomial Action policy via Sparse History-anchored flow (FLASH Policy), which replaces discrete action-chunk generation with continuous Legendre polynomial trajectory representation. Specifically, by fitting expert demonstrations under sparse temporal sampling, FLASH enables a single inference to cover a significantly extended action horizon. To further accelerate generation, FLASH initiates the flow matching process from history polynomial coefficients rather than uninformative Gaussian noise, shortening the transport distance and enabling accurate single-step inference. Moreover, analytic polynomial differentiation directly provides desired velocity feed-forward signals to the torque controller without numerical approximation. Extensive experiments on five simulated and two real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that FLASH achieves state-of-the-art success rates ($\ge 92\%$ across all tasks), a per-episode inference time of $31.40\,ms$ (up to $175\times$ faster than diffusion policies and $18\times$ faster than prior flow matching policies), up to $4\times$ faster training convergence than ACT, and $5\times$ to $7\times$ reduction in controller tracking error compared to discrete-action baselines.

AI.tldr: FLASH Policy replaces iterative denoising with continuous Legendre polynomial trajectory representation, enabling single-step inference for real-time visuomotor control with 175× speedup over diffusion methods and 92%+ success rates across tasks.
AI.motivation: Generative models (diffusion, flow matching) dominate visuomotor policy learning but incur high inference latency due to iterative denoising, which is incompatible with real-time robotic control requirements.
AI.method: Uses continuous Legendre polynomial trajectory representation instead of discrete action-chunk generation; fits expert demonstrations under sparse temporal sampling; initiates flow matching from history polynomial coefficients rather than Gaussian noise; employs analytic polynomial differentiation for velocity feed-forward signals.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art success rates (≥92% across 7 tasks), per-episode inference time of 31.40ms (175× faster than diffusion, 18× faster than prior flow matching), 4× faster training convergence than ACT, and 5-7× reduction in controller tracking error vs. discrete-action baselines.
AI.conclusion: FLASH successfully enables fast, accurate visuomotor policy learning suitable for real-time robotic control, with significant improvements in both inference speed and training efficiency while maintaining high performance.

title: OffsetAxis: UDF Mesh Reconstruction via Offset-Volume Medial Axis Extraction
summary: Unsigned distance fields (UDFs) offer broader modeling capabilities than signed distance fields (SDFs), enabling the representation of shapes with open boundaries, non-manifold structures or mixed curve and surface parts. However, extracting coherent meshes from UDFs is fundamentally harder, as classical grid-based iso-surfacing techniques are not applicable since they require a way to distinguish the inside from the outside of the shape. We introduce OffsetAxis, a new UDF reconstruction pipeline that supports open, non-manifold, and curve-like geometries. Our key insight is that the 0-level set extraction problem can be restated as the extraction of the medial axis of the $α$-offset volume of the UDF. This formulation unlocks mature medial-axis machinery that naturally supports boundaries, non-manifold junctions and curves. To avoid the biases of grid-based techniques, we sample the $α$-offset surface using ray casting and optimize medial balls inside the offset volume with an efficient variant of Variational Medial Axis Sampling. The final mesh is recovered by taking the dual of the connectivity of the medial ball clusters, producing structurally coherent reconstructions for a wide range of topologies. The robustness and versatility of the approach allow it to handle imperfect distance fields, including neural UDFs trained on noisy inputs, the Quasi-Medial Distance Field (Q-MDF), as well as distances computed directly on triangle soups or point clouds. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces more faithful mesh reconstruction and better alignment with the underlying shape structure than prior techniques.

AI.tldr: OffsetAxis: A UDF reconstruction pipeline that converts 0-level set extraction into medial axis extraction of the α-offset volume, enabling coherent mesh reconstruction for open, non-manifold, and curve-like geometries including imperfect distance fields.
AI.motivation: Unsigned Distance Fields (UDFs) offer broader modeling capabilities than Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) by representing shapes with open boundaries, non-manifold structures, and mixed curve/surface parts. However, classical grid-based iso-surfacing fails with UDFs because they lack a clear inside/outside distinction, making mesh extraction fundamentally harder.
AI.method: Key insight: reformulate 0-level set extraction as medial axis extraction of the α-offset volume. The method: (1) samples the α-offset surface using ray casting, (2) optimizes medial balls inside the offset volume with a variant of Variational Medial Axis Sampling, (3) recovers the mesh via the dual of medial ball cluster connectivity.
AI.result: Produces structurally coherent reconstructions across various topologies; handles imperfect distance fields (neural UDFs, Q-MDF, triangle soups, point clouds); demonstrates more faithful mesh reconstruction and better alignment with underlying shape structure than prior techniques.
AI.conclusion: OffsetAxis effectively addresses the fundamental challenge of mesh extraction from UDFs by leveraging mature medial-axis machinery, achieving robust reconstruction quality and versatility that surpasses existing methods.

title: Multi-Agent Cooperative Transportation: Optimal and Efficient Task Allocation and Path Finding
summary: Multi-robot systems are integral to modern logistics, but their capabilities are often limited to tasks executable by individual agents. This paper addresses a critical gap in existing frameworks like Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) and Task Allocation and Path Finding (TAPF), which lack true cooperation for transporting large items that require multiple agents. To this end, we formalise the Cooperative Transportation Task Allocation and Path Finding (CT-TAPF) problem, which integrates team formation, task assignment, and collision-free pathfinding. We present an optimal solver, Cooperative Transportation Task Conflict-Based Search (CT-TCBS), which features a novel Incremental Expansion strategy to tackle the combinatorial explosion inherent in team formation. Recognising the computational cost of optimality, we also develop a family of sub-optimal solvers that employ a global, task-centric perspective, selecting the next task to assign based on a global difficulty metric (Best Task or Worst Task). Our comprehensive empirical evaluation demonstrates three key findings: (1) the incremental expansion strategy significantly outperforms the naive combinatorial approach by successfully pruning the dominant task-allocation search space; (2) we identify a task-conflict expansion dilemma, where sophisticated conflict resolvers effective for large-agent pathfinding subproblems can be detrimental in the integrated CT-TAPF setting; and (3) our proposed sub-optimal solvers establish a new, more efficient frontier on the solution quality-runtime spectrum compared to "nn-" agent-centric baselines. This work provides a foundational framework and a set of effective algorithms for a new, practical class of cooperative multi-agent problems.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the Cooperative Transportation Task Allocation and Path Finding (CT-TAPF) problem, where multiple robots must coordinate to transport large items requiring team effort. The authors developed CT-TCBS, an optimal solver featuring a novel Incremental Expansion strategy to handle combinatorial complexity, plus sub-optimal solvers using global task-centric heuristics. Empirical results show the incremental expansion significantly outperforms naive approaches, reveal a task-conflict expansion dilemma, and establish new efficiency frontiers on solution quality-runtime tradeoffs.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot systems are essential for modern logistics, yet existing frameworks like MAPF and TAPF lack true cooperation capabilities for tasks requiring multiple agents to move large items together. This creates a critical gap in handling real-world scenarios where coordinated effort is necessary, such as transporting furniture, equipment, or large packages that cannot be moved by a single robot.
AI.method: The authors formalized the Cooperative Transportation Task Allocation and Path Finding (CT-TAPF) problem, integrating team formation, task assignment, and collision-free pathfinding. They developed CT-TCBS (Cooperative Transportation Task Conflict-Based Search), an optimal solver using a novel Incremental Expansion strategy to tackle combinatorial explosion in team formation. Additionally, they created sub-optimal solvers employing a global, task-centric perspective with Best Task and Worst Task selection heuristics based on a global difficulty metric.
AI.result: Three key findings emerged: (1) Incremental expansion significantly outperforms naive combinatorial approaches by effectively pruning the dominant task-allocation search space; (2) A task-conflict expansion dilemma was identified where sophisticated conflict resolvers effective for large-agent pathfinding subproblems can be detrimental in the integrated CT-TAPF setting; (3) The proposed sub-optimal solvers establish a new frontier on the solution quality-runtime spectrum, outperforming "nn-" agent-centric baselines in efficiency.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a foundational framework and a set of effective algorithms for cooperative multi-agent problems, bridging a critical gap between individual agent capabilities and true multi-agent cooperation. The algorithms and insights offer practical solutions for logistics and robotics applications where coordinated transportation of large items is required, advancing the field beyond current MAPF and TAPF limitations.

title: LAPS: Improving Incremental LiDAR Mapping using Active Pooling and Sampling for Neural Distance Fields
summary: Neural distance fields offer a compact and continuous representation of 3D geometry, making them attractive for incremental LiDAR mapping. However, their online optimization is vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting, where new observations can degrade previously reconstructed geometry. Replay-based training is commonly used to address this issue, but existing methods typically rely on passive replay buffers and uniform sampling, which can waste memory on redundant observations and under-train poorly constrained regions. We propose LAPS, a replay management framework for incremental neural mapping that improves both replay retention and replay allocation during online updates. LAPS combines reliability-based active pooling to retain reliable historical samples under limited memory with uncertainty-guided active sampling to focus optimization on under-constrained regions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that LAPS consistently improves reconstruction completeness while maintaining competitive geometric accuracy. On Oxford Spires, it improves recall by 4.66 pp and F1-score by 3.79 pp over PIN-SLAM on the Blenheim Palace 05 sequence. We release our open source implementation at: https://github.com/dongjae0107/LAPS.

AI.tldr: LAPS is a replay management framework for incremental neural mapping that combines reliability-based active pooling and uncertainty-guided active sampling to improve replay retention and allocation, achieving better reconstruction completeness while maintaining geometric accuracy.
AI.motivation: Neural distance fields provide compact and continuous 3D geometry representations but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during online optimization. Existing replay-based methods use passive buffers and uniform sampling, which waste memory on redundant observations and under-train poorly constrained regions.
AI.method: LAPS combines reliability-based active pooling (retaining reliable historical samples under limited memory) with uncertainty-guided active sampling (focusing optimization on under-constrained regions) for effective replay management during online updates.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show LAPS consistently improves reconstruction completeness while maintaining competitive geometric accuracy. On Oxford Spires, it improves recall by 4.66 pp and F1-score by 3.79 pp over PIN-SLAM on the Blenheim Palace 05 sequence.
AI.conclusion: LAPS effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting in incremental neural mapping by intelligently managing replay buffers. The proposed approach maintains geometric accuracy while significantly improving reconstruction completeness, with the authors providing an open-source implementation.

title: 3DEditSafe: Defending 3D Editing Pipelines from Unsafe Generation
summary:
Recent advances in 3D generative editing, particularly pipelines based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), have achieved high-fidelity, multi-view-consistent scene manipulation from text prompts. However, we find that these pipelines also introduce new safety risks when unsafe prompts produce edits that are propagated and optimized across views. In this work, we study unsafe generation in 3D editing pipelines and show that such behavior can lead to coherent, undesirable Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content in the final 3D representation.
  To address this, we propose 3DEditSafe, a safety-regularized 3D editing framework that constrains unsafe semantic propagation during optimization. 3DEditSafe combines generation-stage safety guidance with rendered-view 3D safety regularization, safe semantic projection, residue suppression, and mask-aware preservation to steer optimization away from unsafe editing directions. We evaluate our approach on EditSplat scenes using an object-compatible unsafe prompt benchmark and show that 2D safety guidance alone is not consistently sufficient to prevent unsafe 3D edits. 3DEditSafe reduces unsafe semantic alignment and view-level attack success rates, while revealing a safety-quality tradeoff in which stronger unsafe suppression can introduce artifacts or reduce unsafe-prompt fidelity. To our knowledge, this work is the first attempt to study and defend against unsafe generation in text-driven 3D editing pipelines, highlighting the need for safety mechanisms that operate directly on optimized 3D representations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces 3DEditSafe, a safety-regularized framework that constrains unsafe semantic propagation during 3D Gaussian Splatting editing, demonstrating that 2D safety guidance alone is insufficient and that safety-quality tradeoffs exist in 3D editing pipelines.
AI.motivation: Text-driven 3D editing pipelines based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can generate high-fidelity, multi-view-consistent edits but introduce new safety risks when unsafe prompts produce edits that propagate across views, leading to coherent undesirable NSFW content in the final 3D representation.
AI.method: 3DEditSafe combines five key components: (1) generation-stage safety guidance, (2) rendered-view 3D safety regularization, (3) safe semantic projection, (4) residue suppression, and (5) mask-aware preservation to constrain unsafe semantic propagation during optimization and steer it away from unsafe editing directions.
AI.result: The authors evaluated 3DEditSafe on EditSplat scenes using an object-compatible unsafe prompt benchmark, finding that 2D safety guidance alone is not consistently sufficient to prevent unsafe 3D edits. 3DEditSafe reduces unsafe semantic alignment and view-level attack success rates, but reveals a safety-quality tradeoff where stronger unsafe suppression can introduce artifacts or reduce unsafe-prompt fidelity.
AI.conclusion: This work is the first to study and defend against unsafe generation in text-driven 3D editing pipelines, highlighting the need for safety mechanisms that operate directly on optimized 3D representations rather than relying solely on 2D safety guidance.

title: Task-Semantic Graph-Driven Distributed Agent Networking for Underwater Target Tracking
summary: Autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) swarms are emerging as intelligent underwater networks, where each node must sense, communicate, process local data, and make decisions under severe acoustic constraints. Persistent underwater target tracking is a typical task with moving targets, changing communication topology, intermittent acoustic links, and limited observation for each AUV. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a natural candidate for distributed tracking, yet existing studies still lack a unified open-source platform for evaluating different MARL algorithms under six-degree-of-freedom AUV dynamics. In addition, policies trained with raw geometric states and low-level force actions often struggle to represent task phases, observation reliability, link quality, and local cooperation roles. This paper addresses these issues by developing an open-source MARL-AUV platform that integrates DI-engine with a six-degree-of-freedom underwater AUV target-tracking simulator. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first open platform that connects a public MARL training framework with physically modeled AUV swarm-based tasks, and provides a unified experimental protocol for fair training, testing, and comparison of representative RL and MARL algorithms. Based on this platform, we propose STG-MAPPO, a Semantic Task Graph-enhanced variant of Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization. STG-MAPPO builds semantic policy inputs from tracking diagnostics, task phases, observation confidence, link availability, neighbor tracking quality, and local role advantage. A compact semantic task graph links communication-constrained network states to decentralized actor decisions, and a velocity-level action abstraction maps high-level cooperative decisions to executable six-degree-offreedom AUV control inputs.The code is available at https://github.com/dasjsaj/MARL-AUV.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an open-source MARL-AUV platform for evaluating Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning algorithms in 6-DOF AUV swarms for underwater target tracking, along with a novel algorithm called STG-MAPPO that uses semantic task graphs to improve policy representation.
AI.motivation: AUV swarms face severe acoustic constraints, moving targets, changing communication topologies, intermittent links, and limited observations during persistent underwater target tracking. Existing MARL studies lack a unified open-source platform for evaluating algorithms under physically modeled 6-DOF AUV dynamics. Additionally, policies trained with raw geometric states and low-level force actions struggle to represent task phases, observation reliability, link quality, and local cooperation roles.
AI.method: The authors developed an open-source MARL-AUV platform integrating DI-engine with a 6-DOF underwater AUV target-tracking simulator, providing a unified experimental protocol for fair training, testing, and comparison of RL and MARL algorithms. They proposed STG-MAPPO (Semantic Task Graph-enhanced Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization), which builds semantic policy inputs from tracking diagnostics, task phases, observation confidence, link availability, neighbor tracking quality, and local role advantage. A compact semantic task graph links communication-constrained network states to decentralized actor decisions, while a velocity-level action abstraction maps high-level cooperative decisions to executable 6-DOF AUV control inputs.
AI.result: The paper introduces the first open platform connecting a public MARL training framework with physically modeled AUV swarm tasks. STG-MAPPO addresses the limitations of raw geometric state representations by incorporating semantic information about task phases, observation reliability, link quality, and cooperative roles. The code is available at https://github.com/dasjsaj/MARL-AUV.
AI.conclusion: The proposed open-source platform provides a unified experimental protocol for fair training, testing, and comparison of MARL algorithms in underwater AUV swarms. STG-MAPPO demonstrates the benefits of using semantic task graphs and semantic policy inputs to improve performance under communication constraints and complex underwater tracking scenarios.

title: A QUBO Formulation Framework for Kinematic Structure-Based Robot Design Optimization: A Robotic Hand Case Study
comment: This manuscript has been submitted for possible publication. 14 pages, 5 figures
summary: This paper presents a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization-based formulation framework for robot design optimization using kinematic structure-level evaluation metrics. In the proposed framework, classical computation is used to evaluate design-dependent metrics while the resulting combinatorial selection problem is formulated in a structure compatible with quantum annealing-based optimization. A robotic hand is adopted as a representative case study, as its performance is determined by both the individual kinematic characteristics of each finger and interaction terms. The proposed formulation incorporates individual design rewards, overlap workspace interactions, one-hot constraint, and structural dependency penalties into a unified quadratic model. A 27-variable robotic hand design problem is constructed, and simulated annealing is used as a classical baseline to verify the feasibility of the formulation. Quantum annealing is further performed to examine the applicability of the proposed formulation to annealing-based hardware execution. The results show that feasible design combinations satisfying both one-hot selection and pairwise constraints can be obtained, with the observed objective-value range becoming narrower as the number of reads increases. In addition, the formulation process is discussed for other robotic systems. The proposed framework provides a generalized approach for transforming kinematic structure-based robot design problems into combinatorial optimization problems.

AI.tldr: A QUBO-based formulation framework for robot design optimization that transforms kinematic structure-level evaluation metrics into a combinatorial optimization problem compatible with quantum annealing.
AI.motivation: Robot design optimization is challenging due to performance dependencies on both individual kinematic characteristics and interaction terms; the paper aims to provide a generalized approach for transforming these problems into combinatorial optimization formulations.
AI.method: Classical computation evaluates design-dependent metrics, while the combinatorial selection problem is formulated as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model incorporating individual design rewards, overlap workspace interactions, one-hot constraint, and structural dependency penalties. A 27-variable robotic hand case study is constructed and verified using simulated annealing and quantum annealing.
AI.result: Feasible design combinations satisfying both one-hot selection and pairwise constraints are obtained. The objective-value range becomes narrower as the number of reads increases. Both classical simulated annealing and quantum annealing demonstrate the feasibility of the formulation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a generalized approach for transforming kinematic structure-based robot design problems into combinatorial optimization problems, demonstrating applicability to quantum annealing hardware execution.

title: DealMaTe: Multi-Dimensional Material Transfer via Diffusion Transformer
summary: Recently, diffusion-based material transfer methods rely on image fine-tuning or complex architectures with auxiliary networks but face challenges such as text dependency, additional computational costs, and feature misalignment. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{DealMaTe}, using \underline{\textbf{de}}pth, norm\underline{\textbf{a}}l, and \underline{\textbf{l}}ighting images for \underline{\textbf{ma}}terial \underline{\textbf{t}}ransf\underline{\textbf{e}}r. DealMaTe is a simplified diffusion framework that eliminates text guidance and reference networks. We design a lightweight 3D information injection method, Multi-Dim 3D Shader LoRA, which, without modifying the base model weights, enables compatible control conditions and achieves harmonious and stable results. Additionally, we optimize the attention mechanism with Shader Causal Mutual Attention and key-value (KV) caching to reduce inference latency caused by multiple conditions, improve computational efficiency, and achieve high-quality material transfer results with low architectural complexity. Extensive experiments covering a wide variety of objects and lighting conditions consistently demonstrate that DealMaTe achieves remarkable high-fidelity material transfer under arbitrary input materials. The code is available at https://github.com/haha-lisa/DealMaTe.

AI.tldr: DealMaTe is a simplified diffusion framework for material transfer that uses depth, normal, and lighting images instead of text guidance, employing a lightweight Multi-Dim 3D Shader LoRA for 3D information injection and optimized attention mechanisms to achieve high-fidelity results with low computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based material transfer methods rely on image fine-tuning or complex architectures with auxiliary networks, but face challenges such as text dependency, additional computational costs, and feature misalignment.
AI.method: DealMaTe eliminates text guidance and reference networks by using depth, normal, and lighting images. It introduces Multi-Dim 3D Shader LoRA for lightweight 3D information injection without modifying base model weights, and optimizes the attention mechanism with Shader Causal Mutual Attention and key-value (KV) caching to reduce inference latency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across various objects and lighting conditions demonstrate that DealMaTe achieves remarkable high-fidelity material transfer with harmonious and stable results, while significantly reducing computational cost and inference latency compared to complex baselines.
AI.conclusion: DealMaTe successfully achieves high-quality material transfer under arbitrary input materials by simplifying the framework, removing text dependencies, and optimizing attention mechanisms, making it an efficient and effective solution for material transfer tasks.

title: Terrain Consistent Reference-Guided RL for Humanoid Navigation Autonomy
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, intended to submit to Humanoids 2026
summary: We present a method for training reference-guided, perceptive reinforcement learning locomotion policies for humanoid robots in which reference trajectories are modulated in training to be consistent with terrain geometry. Aiming to deploy our method with standard navigation autonomy infrastructure, we synthesize SE(2)-controllable reference trajectories inside the RL training loop, projecting desired footsteps onto valid footholds and adjusting swing-foot and center-of-mass trajectories to match the terrain. The resulting policy exposes a clean SE(2) velocity interface compatible with standard navigation planners. In simulation, environmentally-conditioned references significantly improve reference tracking performance compared to environment agnostic references. On hardware, we integrate the policy with an MPC + control barrier function planner and demonstrate long-horizon (>70m) closed-loop autonomous navigation on the Unitree G1 through outdoor environments containing rough terrain and consecutive flights of stairs, with all sensing and computation onboard.

AI.tldr: A method for training humanoid robots to follow terrain-consistent reference trajectories using reinforcement learning, with SE(2) velocity control interface, showing significant improvements in tracking and successful hardware demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Developing reference-guided, perceptive reinforcement learning locomotion policies for humanoid robots that work with standard navigation infrastructure, focusing on terrain consistency and compatibility with existing navigation planners.
AI.method: Modulating reference trajectories during RL training to match terrain geometry by synthesizing SE(2)-controllable trajectories, projecting desired footsteps onto valid footholds, and adjusting swing-foot and center-of-mass trajectories to align with terrain. The resulting policy exposes a clean SE(2) velocity interface compatible with standard navigation planners.
AI.result: Environmentally-conditioned references significantly improve reference tracking performance over environment-agnostic references. Successfully integrated with MPC + control barrier function planner, demonstrating long-horizon (70m+) closed-loop autonomous navigation on Unitree G1 through outdoor environments with rough terrain and consecutive flights of stairs, with all sensing and computation onboard.
AI.conclusion: The method enables robust, terrain-aware humanoid locomotion that integrates seamlessly with standard navigation systems, achieving reliable long-horizon autonomous navigation in challenging real-world environments.

title: StippleDiffusion: Capacity-Constrained Stippling using Controlled Diffusion
summary: Stipple patterns, point sets whose local density tracks a target image, are traditionally produced by per-density iterative optimizers, which are slow, non-differentiable, and must be re-run from scratch for each new target. Learned alternatives have so far addressed only unconditional point generation; capacity-constrained, image-conditioned stippling has remained out of reach. We present the first diffusion-based sampler that simultaneously satisfies a learned local point-distribution prior and a continuous, image-defined capacity constraint at inference. The method is a ControlNet branch built on top of an optimal-transport-grid point-set diffusion baseline, conditioned on the target density map and a high-resolution image. Two design choices make the combination tractable: training and inference are restricted to the late-stage denoising regime, initialized from a density-weighted rejection sample, and the standard zero-convolution injection is replaced with a sigmoid-gated 1x1 projection that preserves the base model's blue-noise structure under hard density signals. A single trained checkpoint accepts arbitrary target densities at inference, generalizes to point budgets that were not seen during training, and produces stipples in time nearly independent of the output point count. On the Icons-50 benchmark, our learned sampler reaches parity with per-density-optimized baselines on every reported metric while remaining differentiable end-to-end.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based ControlNet sampler for stipple patterns that combines point-distribution prior with image-defined capacity constraints, enabling efficient, differentiable generation conditioned on target density maps.
AI.motivation: Traditional stipple generation using per-density iterative optimizers is slow, non-differentiable, and requires re-running for each new target. Learned alternatives only address unconditional point generation; capacity-constrained, image-conditioned stippling remains unsolved.
AI.method: A ControlNet branch built on optimal-transport-grid point-set diffusion baseline, conditioned on target density map and high-resolution image. Training/inference restricted to late-stage denoising regime, initialized from density-weighted rejection sample, with sigmoid-gated 1x1 projection replacing zero-convolution injection to preserve blue-noise structure.
AI.result: On Icons-50 benchmark, reaches parity with per-density-optimized baselines on all metrics while being differentiable end-to-end. Generalizes to unseen point budgets, with time nearly independent of output point count.
AI.conclusion: First diffusion-based sampler for capacity-constrained, image-conditioned stippling that enables efficient, differentiable generation with arbitrary target densities.

title: Distributed Affine Body Dynamics with Adaptive Consensus
summary: Affine Body Dynamics (ABD) within the Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) framework provides accurate simulation of extremely stiff solids exhibiting near-rigid behavior, with strict non-penetration guarantees. However, IPC's globally coupled barrier constraints hinder scalable execution across multiple GPUs and compute nodes. We propose a distributed formulation of ABD using a consensus-based ADMM scheme. Each compute node solves its local ABD subproblem in parallel, followed by a global consensus step that enforces consistency among shared boundary bodies. The proposed method preserves IPC-level robustness and global consistency under distributed execution. Experiments demonstrate stable convergence, non-penetration, and efficient scaling on large-scale scenes across multiple nodes.

AI.tldr: A distributed consensus-based ADMM formulation of ABD that preserves IPC-level robustness and non-penetration guarantees while enabling scalable parallel execution across multiple GPUs and compute nodes.
AI.motivation: IPC's globally coupled barrier constraints hinder scalable execution across multiple GPUs and compute nodes, despite its accurate simulation of stiff solids with strict non-penetration guarantees.
AI.method: A distributed formulation of ABD using a consensus-based ADMM scheme where each compute node solves its local ABD subproblem in parallel, followed by a global consensus step enforcing consistency among shared boundary bodies.
AI.result: The method preserves IPC-level robustness and global consistency under distributed execution, achieving stable convergence, non-penetration, and efficient scaling on large-scale scenes across multiple nodes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed distributed formulation successfully addresses IPC's scalability challenges while maintaining its robustness guarantees for simulating extremely stiff solids exhibiting near-rigid behavior.

title: SkiP: When to Skip and When to Refine for Efficient Robot Manipulation
summary: Previous imitation learning policies predict future actions at every control step, whether in smooth motion phases or precise, contact-rich operation phases. This uniform treatment is wasteful: most steps in a manipulation trajectory traverse free space and carry little task-relevant information, while a small fraction of \emph{key} steps around contacts, grasps, and alignment demand dense, high-resolution prediction. We propose a novel \emph{action relabeling} mechanism: at each timestep in a skip segment, we replace the behavior cloning target with the action at the entrance of the next key segment, enabling the policy to leap over redundant steps in a single decision. The resulting \textbf{Skip Policy (SkiP)} dynamically leaps over skip segments and intensively refines actions in key segments, within a single unified network requiring no learned skip planner or hierarchical structure. To automatically partition demonstrations into key and skip segments without manual annotation, we introduce \emph{Motion Spectrum Keying} (MSK), a fast, task-agnostic procedure that detects local motion complexity from action signals. Extensive experiments across 72 simulated manipulation tasks and three real-robot tasks show that SkiP reduces executed steps by $15$--$40\%$ while matching or improving success rates across various policy backbones. Project page: \texttt{https://pgq18.github.io/SkiP-page/}.

AI.tldr: SkiP proposes a novel action relabeling mechanism that enables imitation learning policies to dynamically skip over redundant steps in manipulation tasks, reducing execution steps by 15-40% while maintaining or improving success rates.
AI.motivation: Previous imitation learning policies uniformly predict actions at every control step, which is wasteful because most steps in free space carry little task-relevant information, while only key steps around contacts, grasps, and alignment require dense, high-resolution prediction.
AI.method: SkiP consists of two main components: (1) Action relabeling - replacing behavior cloning targets at each timestep in skip segments with the action at the entrance of the next key segment, allowing the policy to leap over redundant steps; (2) Motion Spectrum Keying (MSK) - a task-agnostic procedure that detects local motion complexity from action signals to automatically partition demonstrations into key and skip segments without manual annotation.
AI.result: SkiP reduces executed steps by 15-40% while matching or improving success rates across 72 simulated manipulation tasks and 3 real-robot tasks, tested with various policy backbones.
AI.conclusion: SkiP is a unified network approach that requires no learned skip planner or hierarchical structure, providing an efficient and practical solution for imitation learning in manipulation tasks.

title: Smart target point control for Gaussian Splatting methods
summary: Standard Gaussian splatting methods rely on heuristic densification and pruning to adaptively allocate primitives during training, and the resulting Gaussian count strongly influences both reconstruction quality and runtime. This makes comparisons across methods fragile: improvements can stem from higher representational capacity rather than algorithmic design. A common and naive workaround for this is hard-stopping or budgeting densification/pruning once a target count is reached, which biases training because different methods hit the cap at different times, yielding non-uniform densify/prune exposure across views and uneven point distributions. We propose a target point control scheme that preserves the standard densification window and cadence, but adjusts only the existing densification and opacity-culling hyper-parameters to track a quadratic target count trajectory. This quota-governor reaches the desired count by 15k iterations without abrupt cutoffs, ensuring that all methods and views receive equal densification and pruning cycles, enabling fairer, capacity-matched evaluation.

AI.tldr: A target point control scheme for Gaussian splatting that ensures fair, capacity-matched densification by tracking a quadratic count trajectory instead of hard-stopping, eliminating biases in cross-method comparisons.
AI.motivation: Standard Gaussian splatting methods use heuristic densification and pruning, making comparisons fragile since improvements can stem from higher representational capacity rather than algorithmic design. Hard-stopping densification at target counts biases training as different methods reach caps at different times, causing uneven point distributions and non-uniform densify/prune exposure across views.
AI.method: A target point control scheme that preserves standard densification window and cadence while adjusting densification and opacity-culling hyper-parameters to track a quadratic target count trajectory, reaching the desired count by 15k iterations without abrupt cutoffs.
AI.result: The quota-governor approach ensures all methods and views receive equal densification and pruning cycles, enabling fairer, capacity-matched evaluation by eliminating the bias introduced by hard-stopping at different times.
AI.conclusion: By maintaining consistent densification/pruning exposure across methods and views through a smooth quadratic trajectory, the proposed scheme enables more reliable algorithmic comparisons in Gaussian splatting, where capacity differences have previously confounded performance assessments.

title: KaRMA: A Kinematic Metric for Fine Manipulation Ability in Robotic Hands
summary: Traditional robotic hand metrics focus on static properties such as workspace, manipulability, and grasp stability. However, these metrics do not directly measure dexterity under the standard definition in robotic manipulation: the ability to continuously change an object's pose within the hand while maintaining contact from an initial grasp. We introduce Kinematic Rolling Manipulation Ability (KaRMA), a kinematic-only metric for fine manipulation that quantifies reachable in-hand translation and reorientation of a spherical test object within a two-finger precision pinch through feasible rolling motions. KaRMA enforces joint limits, collision constraints, rolling contact, and antipodal force feasibility, then investigates reachable in-hand object poses via breadth-first search over translation and rotation primitives. KaRMA reports three scores: translational coverage (KaRMA-T), rotational coverage (KaRMA-R), and sensitivity to the initial grasp (KaRMA-S). We evaluate KaRMA on 16 widely used robotic hands and compare against static baselines, showing that KaRMA separates hands that rank identically under static proxies, reveals translation-rotation tradeoffs invisible to existing baselines, and is qualitatively consistent with selected published task benchmarks where Jacobian-based metrics can be misleading.

AI.tldr: KaRMA (Kinematic Rolling Manipulation Ability) is a kinematic-only metric that quantifies reachable in-hand translation and reorientation of a spherical object through feasible rolling motions, providing three scores to evaluate robotic hand dexterity.
AI.motivation: Traditional robotic hand metrics focus on static properties (workspace, manipulability, grasp stability) that do not directly measure dexterity—the ability to continuously change an object's pose while maintaining contact during manipulation.
AI.method: KaRMA enforces joint limits, collision constraints, rolling contact, and antipodal force feasibility, then investigates reachable in-hand object poses via breadth-first search over translation and rotation primitives, reporting three scores: KaRMA-T (translational coverage), KaRMA-R (rotational coverage), and KaRMA-S (sensitivity to the initial grasp).
AI.result: Evaluated on 16 widely used robotic hands, KaRMA separates hands that rank identically under static proxies, reveals translation-rotation tradeoffs invisible to existing baselines, and is qualitatively consistent with selected published task benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: KaRMA provides a more meaningful metric for evaluating robotic hand dexterity in fine manipulation tasks compared to static baselines, with Jacobian-based metrics potentially being misleading.

title: Evaluating Design Video Generation: Metrics for Compositional Fidelity
summary: Generative video models are increasingly used in design animation tasks, yet no standardized evaluation framework exists for this domain. Unlike natural video generation, design animation imposes structured constraints: specific components shall animate with prescribed motion types, directions, speed and timing, while non-animated regions must remain stable and layout structure must be preserved. This paper provides a fully automated evaluation framework organized across four dimensions: layout fidelity, motion correctness, temporal quality, and content fidelity. This eliminates the reliance on subjective human evaluation and establishes a common basis for benchmarking progress in the field.

AI.tldr: A fully automated evaluation framework for generative video models in design animation tasks, organized across four dimensions: layout fidelity, motion correctness, temporal quality, and content fidelity.
AI.motivation: Generative video models are increasingly used in design animation tasks, but no standardized evaluation framework exists. Unlike natural video generation, design animation imposes structured constraints that require precise evaluation.
AI.method: A fully automated evaluation framework organized across four dimensions: layout fidelity, motion correctness, temporal quality, and content fidelity.
AI.result: The framework eliminates reliance on subjective human evaluation and establishes a common basis for benchmarking progress in the field.
AI.conclusion: This automated framework provides standardized evaluation for generative video models in design animation, enabling fair comparison and progress tracking across different models and approaches.

title: NavRL++: A System-Level Framework for Improving Sim-to-Real Transfer in Reinforcement Learning-Based Robot Navigation
summary: Recent years have witnessed significant progress in autonomous navigation using reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches largely emphasize reinforcement learning framework design, such as input representations, action spaces, and reward functions, while providing limited analysis of sim-to-real transfer and insufficient insight into how training strategies affect real-world deployment performance. To bridge this gap, we not only introduce an effective RL framework but also present a complete training and deployment pipeline, along with a systematic empirical study that disentangles the key factors affecting sim-to-real transfer in reinforcement learning-based navigation, including sensor noise, perception failures, system latency, and control response. Building on insights from this analysis, we introduce perturbation-aware fine-tuning, a post-training adaptation strategy that improves transfer robustness by explicitly accounting for empirically identified domain discrepancies. To further mitigate perception degradation and enhance control smoothness in real-world deployment, we propose a Transformer-based temporal reasoning policy that leverages short-horizon observation for navigation control. We quantitatively evaluate how individual sim-to-real perturbations and training design choices impact navigation performance across environments. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed training strategy and policy architecture outperform learning-based baselines in both static and dynamic environments, while achieving performance comparable to optimization-based planners in static settings. We validate our approach through real-world deployment on multiple robotic platforms, including aerial and legged robots, across navigation-centric tasks such as exploration and inspection, demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an RL framework and complete training/deployment pipeline for navigation, presents systematic empirical study on sim-to-real transfer factors, proposes perturbation-aware fine-tuning strategy, and a Transformer-based temporal reasoning policy that outperforms baselines and achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing reinforcement learning approaches for autonomous navigation emphasize framework design (input representations, action spaces, reward functions) but provide limited analysis of sim-to-real transfer and insufficient insight into how training strategies affect real-world deployment performance.
AI.method: 1. Introduces effective RL framework and complete training/deployment pipeline 2. Presents systematic empirical study disentangling sim-to-real transfer factors: sensor noise, perception failures, system latency, control response 3. Proposes perturbation-aware fine-tuning as post-training adaptation strategy 4. Proposes Transformer-based temporal reasoning policy leveraging short-horizon observations for navigation control
AI.result: Quantitative evaluation shows proposed training strategy and policy architecture outperform learning-based baselines in both static and dynamic environments, achieve performance comparable to optimization-based planners in static settings, and demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer when validated on aerial and legged robots across exploration and inspection tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed perturbation-aware fine-tuning strategy and Transformer-based temporal reasoning policy effectively improve sim-to-real transfer robustness and navigation performance in real-world deployments.

title: Wind-Aware Optimal Trajectory Planning for Efficient Gliding of Fixed-Wing Aerial Systems
comment: Accepted for publication at IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2026) held in Vienna
summary: Gliding offers small fixed-wing UAVs extended endurance and silent operation but requires accurate energy management, especially under wind disturbances and obstacle constraints. Traditional Total Energy Control Systems based controllers regulate the trade between potential and kinetic energy reactively, often requiring fine-tuning and trim-conditions knowledge. In this work, we shift the regulation to the planning level and present a nonlinear, multi-cost trajectory planner for small UAV gliders. The method generates $\mathcal{C}^3$ continuous trajectories based on Bernstein polynomials, mapped into control commands through differential flatness, and re-planned online to match experimentally derived sink polar curves. A simulated netto variometer is integrated into the optimization to estimate air mass motion, constraining the glide to energy-balanced states. Consecutive gliding trajectories are linked by cruising segments computed through trajectories initialized on Dubins path-based waypoints, enabling hybrid missions that combine powered and unpowered flight. The approach is validated in CFD simulations and real-world experiments with a fixed-wing platform, showing reliable stabilization of sink rate, airspeed, and glide ratio under wind gusts and in presence of obstacles.

AI.tldr: A nonlinear multi-cost trajectory planner for UAV gliders that uses Bernstein polynomial-based C³ continuous trajectories, differential flatness control mapping, and a simulated netto variometer for energy-balanced glide planning, validated in CFD and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Gliding provides small fixed-wing UAVs with extended endurance and silent operation but demands accurate energy management under wind disturbances and obstacles. Traditional Total Energy Control Systems are reactive, requiring fine-tuning and prior knowledge of trim conditions.
AI.method: A nonlinear multi-cost trajectory planner generates C³ continuous trajectories using Bernstein polynomials, mapped to control commands via differential flatness. It includes online replanning to match sink polar curves and integrates a simulated netto variometer to estimate air mass motion and constrain glide to energy-balanced states. Consecutive gliding trajectories are linked by cruising segments computed via Dubins path-based waypoints, enabling hybrid powered-unpowered missions.
AI.result: Validated through CFD simulations and real-world experiments with a fixed-wing platform, the approach reliably stabilizes sink rate, airspeed, and glide ratio under wind gusts and in the presence of obstacles.
AI.conclusion: The proposed planning-level approach successfully enables hybrid missions combining powered and unpowered flight, offering an alternative to reactive Total Energy Control Systems that eliminates the need for fine-tuning and trim-condition knowledge.

title: Propagating Unsafe Actions in LLM Controlled Multi-Robot Collaboration via Single Robot Compromise
comment: Accepted by the 35th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2026). 9 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as general planners in embodied intelligence, enabling high level coordination and low level task planning for both single robot and multi-robot collaboration. This increasing reliance on embodied LLM planners also raises critical security concerns, since misaligned or manipulated instructions can be translated into physical actions. Prior work has studied such threats in single robot settings, while security risks in LLM controlled multi-robot collaboration, especially those propagated through inter robot communication, remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel attack paradigm for multi-robot system in which the adversary interacts with only a single entry robot. The compromised robot then propagates malicious intent through peer communication, leading to coordinated unsafe actions across the system. Our evaluation, covering high risk dimensions of dereliction of duty, privacy compromise, and public safety hazards, reveals a persistent safety alignment gap in multi-robot planners. We quantify this process with three metrics, obedience, infectiousness, and stealthiness. Experiments demonstrate both persistent attacker control and rapid propagation: obedience reaches 1.00 in the strongest cases, and infectiousness rises to 0.90. Notably, the attack is highly efficient, requiring as few as 3.0 rounds to compromise all the robots while maintaining a stealthiness score of 0.81. Prior work has focused on single robot settings, leaving multi-robot security vulnerabilities unaddressed.

title: MyoChallenge 2025: A New Benchmark for Human Athletic Intelligence
summary: Athletic performance represents the pinnacle of human motor intelligence, demanding rapid choices, precise control, agility, and coordinated physical execution. Replicating this seamless combination of capabilities remains elusive in current artificial intelligence and robotic systems. Concurrently, understanding the biological mastery of these movements is hindered because complex muscle coordination is rarely measured in vivo due to the limitations of physical equipment. To bridge this fundamental gap in understanding, MyoChallenge at NeurIPS 2025 established a pioneering benchmark for motor control intelligence in sports, leveraging high-fidelity musculoskeletal models within physics simulation combined with machine learning-driven algorithms. The competition introduces two distinct tracks emphasizing either upper or lower limbs control: a table tennis rally task utilizing a biomechanic upper limb composed of an arm with a hand and a trunk; and a soccer penalty kick using a biomechanic model of legs and a trunk. Marking the fourth iteration of the MyoChallenge series, this event attracted almost 70 teams and over 560 submissions globally, uniting a diverse community ranging from physicians and neuroscientists to machine learning experts. The competition facilitated the development of several state-of-the-art control algorithms for a musculoskeletal system capable of sports agility, leveraging techniques such as physics-based motion planners, on-policy behaviour cloning, hierarchical planning, and muscle synergies. By integrating standardized tasks and physiologically realistic models into the open-source framework of MyoSuite, MyoChallenge'25 serves as a reproducible and reusable testbed to accelerate interdisciplinary research across machine learning, biomechanics, sports science, and neuroscience. Project page: https://www.myosuite.org//myochallenge/myochallenge-2025.

AI.motivation: Current AI and robotic systems cannot replicate the seamless combination of rapid decision-making, precise control, agility, and coordinated execution required for athletic performance. Additionally, biological understanding of complex muscle coordination is limited due to the difficulty of measuring these movements in vivo with existing equipment.
AI.method: The competition leverages high-fidelity musculoskeletal models within physics simulation combined with machine learning algorithms. Two distinct tracks were introduced: table tennis rally using an upper limb biomechanic model (arm, hand, trunk) and soccer penalty kick using a lower limb model (legs and trunk). The competition attracted 70 teams with over 560 submissions, and successful approaches utilized techniques including physics-based motion planners, on-policy behavior cloning, hierarchical planning, and muscle synergies.

The MyoSuite framework now provides a standardized, reproducible, and reusable testbed that integrates physiologically realistic models with open-source tools.
AI.conclusion: MyoChallenge'25 successfully bridges the gap between machine learning, biomechanics, sports science, and neuroscience by creating a comprehensive benchmark. This accelerates interdisciplinary research and enables the development of AI systems that can perform complex athletic movements previously only achievable by humans.

title: PCASim: Promptable Closed-loop Adversarial Simulation for Urban Traffic Environment
summary: Real-world autonomous driving, particularly in urban environments with numerous corner cases, requires rigorous testing to ensure product safety and robustness. However, few studies have explored integrating adversarial scenario generation with the training of safety agents in closed-loop testing, enabling efficient co-evolution and mutual enhancement of both. To address this challenge, an adversarial behavior knowledge repository is constructed by applying rule-based filtering to an open-source dataset, combined with knowledge retrieval modules tailored for simulation environments. A large language model (LLM) is employed to integrate knowledge-, data-, and adversarial-driven approaches, generating safety-critical traffic scenarios customized to user needs. Additionally, while evaluating the generated scenarios, we employ reinforcement learning models to train the behaviors of different types of vehicles, thereby enriching scenario diversity beyond existing datasets while preserving realism. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the accuracy of domain-specific language generation by 12\%. Moreover, the success rate of newly generated scenario transformations increases by 8\%, while obstacle-avoidance capability is enhanced by 30\%. For the complete manuscript, please refer to: https://zhenhaooo.github.io/PCASim.github.io/

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework that integrates adversarial scenario generation with safety agent training in closed-loop testing for autonomous driving. It uses an LLM-driven approach combined with knowledge repositories and reinforcement learning to generate realistic safety-critical traffic scenarios and co-evolve with safety agents, improving scenario diversity and vehicle behavior evaluation.

Few existing studies have explored integrating adversarial scenario generation with safety agent training in closed-loop testing to enable efficient co-evolution between the two.
AI.method: The authors construct an adversarial behavior knowledge repository by applying rule-based filtering to open-source datasets with simulation-tailored retrieval modules. They employ a large language model (LLM) to integrate knowledge-, data-, and adversarial-driven approaches for generating safety-critical traffic scenarios. Additionally, reinforcement learning models are used to train vehicle behaviors during scenario evaluation to enrich scenario diversity while preserving realism.

title: Feedback World Model Enables Precise Guidance of Diffusion Policy
summary: World models aim to improve robotic decision making by predicting the consequences of actions. However, in practice, their predictions often become unreliable once the robot encounters states outside the training distribution, limiting their effectiveness at deployment. We observe that execution itself provides a natural but underutilized signal: after each action, the robot directly observes the true next state, revealing the mismatch between predicted and actual outcomes. Building on this insight, we propose feedback world model, a new paradigm that closes the loop between prediction and observation at inference time. Instead of treating the world model as a static open-loop predictor, our method maintains a lightweight feedback state that is updated online to iteratively correct future predictions, compensating for model errors using real-time observations without additional training data or parameter updates. We show that this process can be interpreted as a latent-space observer and admits convergence guarantees under mild conditions. We further introduce action-aware guidance to better translate corrected predictions into control by emphasizing action-controllable components while suppressing irrelevant variations. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, Robomimic, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that our method substantially improves both prediction accuracy and policy performance under distribution shift. In particular, it reduces world model prediction error by up to 76.4% and improves out-of-distribution (OOD) success rate by 30%. These results show that incorporating real-time feedback at inference time provides a simple yet powerful alternative to static world modeling.

AI.tldr: A feedback world model closes the prediction-observation loop at inference time by maintaining a lightweight online-updated feedback state that corrects future predictions using real-time observations, achieving up to 76.4% reduction in prediction error and 30% improvement in OOD success rate across LIBERO-Plus, Robomimic, and real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: World models for robotic decision making become unreliable when encountering states outside the training distribution (distribution shift), limiting deployment effectiveness. The authors observe that execution itself provides a natural but underutilized signal - after each action, robots directly observe the true next state, revealing mismatches between predicted and actual outcomes.
AI.method: The Feedback World Model paradigm maintains a lightweight feedback state that is updated online after each action to iteratively correct future predictions. This process compensates for model errors using real-time observations without additional training data or parameter updates. The method can be interpreted as a latent-space observer with convergence guarantees under mild conditions. Additionally, action-aware guidance emphasizes action-controllable components while suppressing irrelevant variations to better translate corrected predictions into control.
AI.result: Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, Robomimic, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate substantial improvements: world model prediction error reduced by up to 76.4%, and out-of-distribution (OOD) success rate improved by 30%. The method outperforms static world modeling approaches.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating real-time feedback at inference time provides a simple yet powerful alternative to static world modeling for robotic decision making under distribution shift. The approach achieves significant performance gains without requiring additional training data or parameter updates.

title: Learning Dynamic Pick-and-Place for a Legged Manipulator
comment: Accepted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 2026
summary: Legged manipulators extend robotic capabilities beyond static manipulation by integrating agile locomotion with versatile arm control. However, achieving precise manipulation while maintaining coordinated locomotion remains a major challenge. This work presents a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for dynamic pick-and-place tasks using a quadruped equipped with a 6-DOF robotic arm. The framework incorporates an explicit mass estimation module enabling adaptive whole-body control for objects with varying weights. In simulation, the system achieves an 86.05% success rate with payloads up to 2.3 kg. The approach is further validated through real-world experiments across six representative scenarios with controlled variations in object physical properties (size and mass) and task heights. Specifically, within a wide vertical workspace ranging from ground level to 1.1~m-high tabletops, the system demonstrates an average success rate of 73.3% for payloads up to 1.3 kg, with an average execution time of 4.06 s. Unlike prior works that handle lightweight objects and execute pick-and-place motions with slow, piecewise motions, the proposed framework exploits concurrent locomotion and manipulation for dynamic, continuous execution. These results demonstrate the potential of quadrupedal mobile manipulators for adaptive, whole-body pick-and-place with heavier payloads and extended workspaces.

title: Hierarchical and Holistic Open-Vocabulary Functional 3D Scene Graphs for Indoor Spaces
summary: Functional 3D scene graphs offer a versatile and flexible representation for 3D scene understanding and robotic manipulation, defined by object nodes, interactive elements, and functional relationship edges. However, their potential remains underexplored due to the limited coverage of existing benchmarks and the overly straightforward design of previous pipelines, which primarily focus on large-scale furniture but lack of hierarchical structures. Therefore, in this work, we extend the benchmark coverage by introducing dense tabletop objects and explicit multi-level functional relationships. This expansion introduces critical challenges involving small-scale, dense, and similar instances, with lack of visual anchoring in relational reasoning, instance confusion during cross-frame fusion, and attribution uncertainty under dynamic viewpoints. To address these issues, we propose an open-vocabulary pipeline based on 2D visual grounding and 3D graph optimization. Specifically, we anchor fine-grained functional edges from 2D visual evidence, and associate nodes across frames in 3D using multiple cues. Furthermore, edge association is formulated as temporal graph optimization, integrating evidence accumulation, entropy regularization, and temporal smoothing to robustly determine the functional connections of each node. Finally, global hierarchy shaping is performed to recover the hierarchical graph structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can reliably infer functional 3D scene graphs in challenging real-world scenes, thereby further unlocking their potential for practical applications.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an open-vocabulary pipeline for constructing functional 3D scene graphs with dense tabletop objects and multi-level functional relationships, addressing challenges like small-scale instances, visual anchoring, instance confusion, and attribution uncertainty through 2D visual grounding and 3D graph optimization with temporal smoothing.
AI.motivation: Existing functional 3D scene graphs suffer from limited benchmark coverage (primarily large-scale furniture) and lack hierarchical structures, making it difficult to explore their full potential for scene understanding and robotic manipulation.
AI.method: The proposed method combines 2D visual grounding with 3D graph optimization. Key components include: anchoring fine-grained functional edges from 2D visual evidence, associating nodes across frames using multiple cues, formulating edge association as temporal graph optimization with evidence accumulation, entropy regularization, and temporal smoothing, and performing global hierarchy shaping to recover hierarchical graph structure.

AI.conclusion: By successfully addressing the challenges of dense tabletop objects and multi-level functional relationships, the proposed approach unlocks the potential of functional 3D scene graphs for practical applications in scene understanding and robotic manipulation.

title: Lamarckian Inheritance in Dynamic Environments: How Key Variables Affect Evolutionary Dynamics
summary: The co-optimization of a robot's body and brain presents a coupled challenge: the morphology constrains which control strategies are effective, while the control determines how well the morphology performs. To address this, we combine morphology optimization as evolution with controller optimization as lifetime learning, utilizing Lamarckian inheritance to transfer learned controller parameters from parent to offspring. In dynamic environments, existing literature presents conflicting evidence: while traditional evolutionary theory often suggests Lamarckian inheritance lacks benefit, recent studies in evolutionary robotics indicate it can improve performance. We hypothesize that this is because previous works have not included all relevant variables with dynamic environments. In this work, we show that the benefit of Lamarckian inheritance depends on two variables: how conflicting the environmental changes are to robot control, and the predictability of those changes for the robotic agent. Using virtual soft robots and two different learning approaches, Bayesian optimization and reinforcement learning, we show that Lamarckian inheritance only underperforms Darwinian inheritance when the changes are both conflicting and unpredictable. We find that adding a sensor to detect environmental changes restores the benefits for Lamarckian inheritance in conflicting environments, by allowing robotic agents to predict the need for a different behavior, thereby generalizing their control.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates when Lamarckian inheritance provides benefits in co-optimizing robot body and brain within dynamic environments, finding it only underperforms Darwinian inheritance when environmental changes are both conflicting and unpredictable, while adding sensors to detect changes restores its benefits.
AI.motivation: The co-optimization of robot morphology and control presents a coupled challenge where morphology constrains control strategies and control determines morphology performance. Existing literature presents conflicting evidence about whether Lamarckian inheritance is beneficial in dynamic environments, with traditional evolutionary theory suggesting it lacks benefit, while recent evolutionary robotics studies indicate it can improve performance.
AI.method: The study combines morphology optimization (evolution) with controller optimization (lifetime learning) using virtual soft robots and two learning approaches: Bayesian optimization and reinforcement learning. The researchers systematically vary two key variables: how conflicting environmental changes are to robot control, and the predictability of those changes. They also test the addition of sensors to detect environmental changes.
AI.result: Lamarckian inheritance only underperforms Darwinian inheritance when environmental changes are both conflicting and unpredictable. When environmental changes are either predictable or not conflicting, Lamarckian inheritance performs at least as well as Darwinian inheritance. Adding a sensor to detect environmental changes restores the benefits of Lamarckian inheritance in conflicting environments by enabling robotic agents to predict the need for different behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The benefits of Lamarckian inheritance depend on two variables: the conflict level of environmental changes to robot control and their predictability for the robotic agent. Environmental sensing can mitigate limitations of Lamarckian inheritance by enabling better behavioral generalization, suggesting that incorporating sensors can help overcome the challenges of conflicting and unpredictable environmental dynamics in robot evolution.

title: A Topology-Aware Spatiotemporal Handover Framework for Continuous Multi-UAV Tracking
summary: The integration of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles(UAVs) into Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) offers synoptic visibility for traffic monitoring, yet scalable deployment is hindered by trajectory fragmentation, where vehicle identity persistence is lost across multi-UAV Fields of View (FOV). While state-of-the-art frameworks excel in optimizing local trajectory extraction and stability for single-drone imagery, they often function as isolated data silos that generate disjointed trajectories, thereby precluding network-level analysis such as Origin-Destination estimation. This paper presents a real-time Multi-Camera Multi-Vehicle Tracking (MCMT) system designed to handle global identity persistence. Addressing the visual ambiguity and computational cost of appearance-based Re-Identification (Re-ID) in nadir views, we introduce a lightweight Topology-Based Spatiotemporal Handover mechanism. We implement a high-throughput parallel pipeline leveraging YOLO11 and ByteTrack to process concurrent 4K streams. Our core contribution is a deterministic queue-based matching algorithm that utilizes geometric overlaps and virtual lane discretization to predictively manage identity handover via FIFO queues. Experimental results on complex urban environments, including intersections and merging traffic, demonstrate a Handover Success Rate (HOSR) of 99.8% in continuous traffic flows, significantly outperforming Re-ID baselines (74.1%) while validating edge deployment feasibility. The source code is available at https://github.com/JYe9/multi-camera-multi-vehicle-tracking-system.

Existing frameworks operate as isolated data silos generating disjointed trajectories, precluding network-level analysis such as Origin-Destination estimation.
AI.method: The paper introduces a lightweight Topology-Based Spatiotemporal Handover mechanism addressing visual ambiguity and computational costs of appearance-based Re-ID in nadir views. A high-throughput parallel pipeline uses YOLO11 and ByteTrack for concurrent 4K stream processing. The core contribution is a deterministic queue-based matching algorithm utilizing geometric overlaps and virtual lane discretization to predictively manage identity handover via FIFO queues.
